**Relative Strength (IBD RS rating)**
- IBD RS Rating = 1-99 percentile rank of a stock's price performance over the last 12 months vs. all stocks, with the most recent quarter double-weighted (common replication: RS = 0.4×ROC(63) + 0.2×ROC(126) + 0.2×ROC(189) + 0.2×ROC(252), then percentile-ranked). O'Neil: buy 80+; Minervini: 70+ minimum. — [TradingView Minervini Scanner (MarketSmith-style RS)](https://www.tradingview.com/script/y43c2PL9-Minervini-Scanner-MarketSmith-RS-up-to-40-tickers) [F]; formula weights [K] (common public replication, not an IBD disclosure).

**Volume and moving averages**
- Breakout volume should be at least 40-50% above the 50-day average (O'Neil); dry-up of volume in the handle/final contraction signals supply exhaustion; distribution = heavy-volume down days. [K]
- 50/150/200-DMA stack is the core of the Trend Template above; Weinstein's 30-week MA ≈ 150-day MA. — [Chartmill SEPA](https://www.chartmill.com/documentation/trading-and-investing/methodologies/523-SEPA-Explained-Mark-Minervinis-Specific-Entry-Point-Analysis-System) [F]

body:
`insight:buffett-mr-market-fear-greed` | confidence: verified | date: 1988-02-29

1986 letter: 'we simply attempt to be fearful when others are greedy and to be greedy only when others are fearful', followed by 'As this is written, little fear is visible in Wall Street. Instead, euphoria prevails' (written months before the Oct-1987 crash). 1987 letter retells Graham's parable: Mr. Market 'appears daily and names a price', has 'incurable emotional problems', 'doesn't mind being ignored', and 'the more manic-depressive his behavior, the better for you.' Warning: 'Mr. Market is there to serve you, not to guide you. It is his pocketbook, not his wisdom, that you will find useful ... it will be disastrous if you fall under his influence.' 1997 'final exam': a lifetime net saver should welcome lower prices - 'they are elated when stock prices rise and depressed when they fall' is backwards for net buyers. 2008 letter in the crash: 'Price is what you pay; value is what you get' (Graham), 'Whether we're talking about socks or stocks, I like buying quality merchandise when it is marked down', and 'Beware the investment activity that produces applause; the great moves are usually greeted by yawns.' Actionable: for an Indian SIP-stage investor, falling markets are a pay raise; pre-write buy lists with prices so panic periods (Mar-2020, 2008, 2013 taper) trigger action, not paralysis.

Sources:
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1986.html
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1987.html
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1997.html
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/2008ltr.pdf

  GitHub → `aditya-bad/fein` → Settings → General → Default branch → `claude/focused-brahmagupta-g3hraq`.
  *Why:* new sessions then load the memory automatically. Without this, a new session starts blank.

- [ ] **2. YouTube / podcast transcript access.**
  For example a **Supadata** API key (supadata.ai) or a similar YouTube-transcript API.

  *Why:* YouTube blocks automated access from here. This unlocks investor interviews, AGM recordings,
  concall audio, Valuepickr meetups, US podcasts (Invest Like the Best, Acquired, etc.).

- [ ] **3. Screener.in account** (premium with export is ideal).
  *Why:* custom screens, full 10-year history exports, and concall AI summaries need a login.
  Option: create a separate account for research.

- [ ] **4. A connection to an Indian internet location** (your computer via Claude's Remote Control, or an India-based machine).
  *Why:* Grid-India power data, e-way bills, ports, steel and data.gov.in block foreign IP addresses.
  These are leading indicators for whole sectors.

body:
**False alarm: HAL's 227 receivable days, negative CFO and salary borrowings** (`case_study:false-alarm-hal-receivable-days`, single-source). FLAGS: debtor days 144 (FY15) -> 227 (FY19) -> 191 (FY20); CFO negative FY17-19 (-Rs 404 cr, -748, -7,700 cr) while PAT was ~Rs 2,000-2,600 cr; borrowings rose from Rs 80 cr (FY16) to Rs 5,927 cr (FY20), reportedly partly to pay salaries while the Defence Ministry delayed payments; inventory days 800+. CONTEXT: the debtor was the Government of India, a sovereign that delays but does not default; HAL was a near-monopoly supplier of military aircraft and helicopters with a multi-year order book; the delay was a budget-timing issue, visible in Defence Ministry statements. When the dues were cleared, CFO swung to Rs 15,263 cr (FY21) and borrowings fell to ~Rs 50 cr. P/E was 6-14 in 2020-22, so the market priced the flag as real. Stock: low ~Rs 251 (2020) -> Rs 4,762 (Nov 2026), ~19x. LESSON: receivable days must be read with the counterparty's credit quality and the reason for the delay. High receivables from a sovereign or AAA customer with a known payment backlog differ from receivables owed by related parties or unnamed foreign distributors (Gitanjali, PC Jeweller, Cox & Kings).

**False alarm: Amazon's missing profits and heavy capex** (`case_study:false-alarm-amazon-no-profits-capex`, verified). FLAGS: net losses through 2002, near-zero GAAP margins for most of 1997-2015, P/E meaningless or in the hundreds, rising capex (fulfilment centres, then AWS data centres); FCF negative again in 2021-22 during a warehouse over-build [2021-22 FCF magnitudes from memory, unverified]. CONTEXT: (1) negative working capital: customers paid Amazon before Amazon paid suppliers, so growth released cash; (2) management explicitly targeted FCF per share, not EPS (1997 letter); (3) expenses that looked like opex (Prime shipping, AWS R&D) were investments with high incremental returns; (4) AWS, broken out only in 2015, was a hidden high-margin segment. IPO $18 in 1997 = ~$0.075 split-adjusted -> ~$188 (Jul 2021), ~2,500x, through a -94% drawdown (1999-2001). WHERE THE FLAG WAS RIGHT: in 1999-2001 the valuation was absurd and the stock lost 94%; the business flag (no profits) was false, the price flag was true. LESSON: when reported profit is suppressed by deliberate reinvestment, look at gross profit growth, CFO, working-capital sign and segment economics; but a false business flag does not protect you from a valuation crash.
